text.title: EARS Pattern Routing Tree
text.summary: First gate: is this a system response to a condition at all? Most rejected candidates are goals, invariants or quality adjectives and belong in another file. Only after the gate does keyword selection apply.

decision-tree.root-question: Does the candidate describe something a named component of the system DOES, in response to a condition or as a standing property?

conclusion.verdict: STOP. Not a requirement. Move to roadmap.md success metrics with a measured target and a measurement window. EARS has no form for a goal and dressing one in `shall` makes it look checked when it is not.
STOP. Move to project-spec/. An invariant (`an Invoice belongs to exactly one Order`) is a fact about the model, not a behaviour, and has no trigger to hang a pattern on.
Rewrite into a measurable system response or drop it. `intuitive`, `modern`, `robust` pass the grammar and mean nothing; if no threshold, unit or observable exists, there is no requirement here yet.
Record `ears_pattern: n-a` plus a one-line `ears_pattern_na_reason`. Explicit and countable. Note: an FR may never take this route — f3 in the output contract forbids it.
Split into two identifiers first, then classify each half separately. Classification of a bundled statement is meaningless.

GENERATE, do not detect. Happy-path step → `When <action>, the <component> shall <expected result>`; negative-path Trigger/Expected-UX pair → `If <trigger>, then the <component> shall <expected UX>`; Preconditions → prepend `While …`; the flow's Playwright spec becomes verification_method. Ask only for the component name, once per flow.

Optional-feature: `Where <feature is included>, the <system name> shall <system response>`. `Where` means this deployment has the feature at all; if the feature exists everywhere and is merely switched on right now, that is `While` instead. This confusion is the most common misclassification after if/when.
Unwanted-behaviour: `If <trigger>, then the <system name> shall <system response>`. The `then` is obligatory — it is the only second keyword in the notation and the parser depends on it.
Event-driven: `When <trigger>, the <system name> shall <system response>`. An event is instantaneous and expected in normal operation.
State-driven: `While <precondition(s)>, the <system name> shall <system response>`. A state persists; if it fires once and is over, it was an event.

Ubiquitous: `The <system name> shall <system response>` — then challenge it. Most requirements are not ubiquitous; things that look universal usually have an unstated trigger. The linter emits I113 on every ubiquitous classification for exactly this reason.

Overlay, not alternative: Complex is legal, but the clauses must run Where ≺ While ≺ When ≺ If/Then with non-decreasing rank, at most one each of where/when/if, and `then` immediately before the actor. Past three clauses the sentence is worse than a table — lift the preconditions into a state machine and write one requirement per transition.
